content: Lomatium is a genus comprising 70 to 80 species of perennial herbs that are indigenous to the western regions of North America. Several species within this genus, such as Lomatium cous, Lomatium geyeri, and Lomatium macrocarpum, are commonly referred to as biscuit roots due to their starchy, edible roots. These roots have historically served as traditional food sources for Native American communities. They were consumed either cooked or dried and subsequently ground into flour. The flavor of these roots has been described as resembling celery, parsnip, or even stale biscuits. The roots of certain species, including Lomatium dissectum, have been utilized in herbal medicine, particularly for the treatment of coughs and upper respiratory infections. Research conducted by the University of British Columbia has demonstrated that extracts derived from Lomatium dissectum exhibit efficacy in immobilizing Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium in laboratory settings. However, the effectiveness of these extracts in human subjects has not yet been evaluated. It is important to note that this plant family is well-known for including members that are highly toxic. Selected species within the genus include: Lomatium ambiguum, Lomatium bicolor, Lomatium bradshawii, Lomatium brandegei, Lomatium californicum, Lomatium canbyi, Lomatium columbianum, Lomatium cous, Lomatium cusickii, Lomatium cuspidatum, Lomatium dissectum, Lomatium donnellii, Lomatium farinosa, Lomatium foeniculaceum, Lomatium geyeri, Lomatium gormanii, Lomatium grayi, Lomatium greenmanii, Lomatium hallii, Lomatium hambleniae, Lomatium hendersonii, Lomatium idahoense, Lomatium laevigatum, Lomatium leptocarpum, Lomatium macrocarpum, Lomatium martindalei, Lomatium minus, Lomatium nevadense, Lomatium nudicaule, Lomatium oreganum, Lomatium orogenioides, Lomatium rollinsii, Lomatium roseanum, Lomatium salmoniflorum, Lomatium serpentinum, Lomatium suksdorfii, Lomatium thompsonii, Lomatium triternatum, Lomatium tuberosum, Lomatium utriculatum, and Lomatium vaginatum.
